title: Sort with evidence, not vibes
summary: Implement a stable merge sort, choose the right ordering rule, and reason about comparison lower bounds.

scenario.briefing: The advising queue is sorted by priority and then by name. The current report uses an unstable shortcut, so students with equal priority change order between runs. Implement a stable merge sort and explain why the comparison rule is part of correctness.

objectives.description: Implement a stable merge sort with a comparator.
Choose stability when the product requires it.
Explain comparison lower bounds and stability trade-offs.

hints: Split the array until each piece has zero or one element.
Merge two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller head.
When values compare equal, take from the left half to preserve stability.
Recurse on both halves, merge, and return a new array.

misconceptions.description: Returning the input unchanged instead of sorting.
misconceptions.feedback: The result must be ordered by the comparator. Returning the input preserves the original order.

misconceptions.description: Taking from the right half on equal keys.
misconceptions.testDescription: Preserves input order for equal scores.
misconceptions.feedback: Stability requires taking from the left half when comparator values tie.

misconceptions.description: Assuming every sort implementation is stable.
misconceptions.feedback: Stability is a property of the algorithm, not a language guarantee across every implementation. Choose or verify it explicitly.

misconceptions.description: Claiming comparison sorting can always beat n log n.
misconceptions.feedback: A comparison sort needs about n log n comparisons in the worst case. Linear time requires extra assumptions such as a bounded key range.

sections.title: Divide, sort, merge
sections.body: Merge sort splits the input in half, sorts each half recursively, and merges the two sorted halves in linear time. The recursion has log n levels, so the total work is O(n log n).

sections.title: Stability is a visible rule
sections.body: A stable sort preserves the input order of elements that compare equal. When two students share a priority, stability keeps their arrival order. The merge step preserves it by taking the left element on a tie.

sections.title: Comparison sorting has a floor
sections.body: Comparison-based sorting needs about n log n comparisons in the worst case. Counting or radix approaches can beat that only when keys have a bounded, known structure.

options.label: Every sort is stable by default

quiz.explanation: A stable sort keeps equal elements in their input order. Not every sort or library implementation guarantees it.

steps.title: Sorting trade-offs
hints: Think about the number of comparisons in the worst case.
Stability and in-place operation trade memory for behavior.
A bounded integer key allows a different algorithm.
Select n log n, stability, and linear-time special cases; reject guaranteed linear comparison sorting.

statements.label: Comparison sorting has an O(n log n) worst-case lower bound.
Stability preserves the input order of elements that compare equal.
Merge sort usually needs O(n) extra memory for the merge.
Counting or radix sort can run in linear time when keys have a bounded range.
A comparison sort can always be made linear with a better loop.

steps.explanation: Comparison sorting pays a logarithmic factor. Linear-time sorts rely on key structure, and stability is a behavioral choice with a memory cost.
